365.title: Mostly quiet
365.hook: speak rarely and only what's needed, and not about people (Enchiridion 33)
365.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism treat silence as their default in conversation and make a habit of not discussing absent people, especially not blaming, praising or comparing them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the diviner, and the one question you never need to ask. Your line was reason has already answered. Which duty did you do without waiting? Day three hundred sixty-five.

Three hundred sixty-five. A whole calendar's worth of days. Worth one breath of its own. Now, a test. Think back over yesterday's conversations, every one of them, the kitchen, the office, the group chat. How many were about someone who wasn't there? It's not a trick question, and the answer can be a little uncomfortable. The handbook's thirty-third section is a long one, a set of small rules for how a person of character talks, laughs and listens. We'll take it over a few days. It starts with the mouth. Today: mostly quiet.
screen: `THREE HUNDRED SIXTY-FIVE.` → `HOW MUCH TALK WAS ABOUT SOMEONE ELSE?` → `MOSTLY QUIET.`

segments.voice: First, the frame. Section thirty-three begins: decide now on a certain character and pattern for yourself, and keep to it, whether you're alone or with other people. Everything after is a sketch of that character. Second, the first stroke of the sketch. Let silence be the general rule, Epictetus says. Or say only what's needed, and in few words. That's not a vow of silence. It's a default, like a resting position. Third, what to skip when you do talk. Rarely, when the moment calls for it, speak, he says, but not about the ordinary topics: gladiators, horse races, athletes, food and drink. Those were the everyday topics of his world, he implies. Translate them into today and you'll recognize the list. Epictetus isn't banning sports. He's noticing how many hours of a life can go into conversation that leaves nobody changed. Fourth, and above all, not about people. Don't blame them, he says, don't praise them, don't compare them. That's the one he leans on hardest. And then a gentler line: if you can, turn your friends' conversation toward something worthwhile, and if you find yourself among strangers, keep quiet. Why would a Stoic care so much? Because talk about absent people is almost always talk about things outside our control: what they did, what they're like, what they deserve. It feeds judgment and envy, and it rarely helps the person being discussed. Mostly quiet isn't cold. It leaves room for the conversations that matter.
screen: `CHOOSE A CHARACTER, AND KEEP IT.` · `SILENCE AS THE DEFAULT.` · `SKIP THE GLADIATORS AND HORSE RACES.` · `ABOVE ALL, NOT ABOUT PEOPLE.` · then, large: `MOSTLY QUIET.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let the noise of the day thin out. Now picture the moment, later today, when a conversation turns toward someone who isn't there. There may be a pull to it, the little thrill of the story. See yourself letting it pass. Maybe you say nothing. Maybe you ask the other person how they're doing instead. Notice what it feels like not to add a word. Then just rest in the quiet you're sitting in now. The bell holds the time.
Mostly quiet. Epictetus' first rule for a person of character: silence by default, few words when needed, and not about people. Today's word.
Your line: let silence be the rule. When talk turns to someone who isn't there today, skip one piece of gossip. Let it pass, or change the subject. Day three hundred sixty-five.

silence is the general rule; speak when needed, in few words.
he warns against praising absent people, not just blaming them
blaming, praising and comparing are all on his list.

options: join in, it's harmless.

fork.reveal: he says to turn friends' conversation toward what's fitting if you can, and among strangers simply to keep quiet.

what it means: silence is a default, few words when needed, and above all no talk that blames, praises or compares people.
what a scholar hears: section thirty-three, a long run of small rules, opens by asking you to choose a character and keep it, alone or in company.

366.title: Yes means yes
366.hook: don't laugh much or loudly, and avoid swearing oaths when you can (Enchiridion 33)
366.carry: a word that doesn't need help
366.howItsDone: Some people on a Stoic path avoid oaths and emphatic promises and try to keep their plain word instead; Quakers and some other Christian communities affirm rather than swear.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first rule of section thirty-three, silence by default, and not about people. Your line was let silence be the rule. Did you let a piece of gossip pass? Day three hundred sixty-six.

I swear I'll be there. I swear on my mother. Hand on heart, I promise. We stack these up when we want to be believed, and the funny thing is, the more we pile on, the less sure everyone gets. Someone who says I swear three times in one sentence can end up being the one people double-check. Section thirty-three keeps going with its sketch of a person of character, and today it gets to two small habits: how you laugh, and how you promise. Today: yes means yes.
screen: `I SWEAR. I SWEAR ON MY MOTHER.` → `THE MORE WE PILE ON, THE LESS SURE.` → `YES MEANS YES.`

segments.voice: First, laughter. Don't laugh much, Epictetus says, or at many things, or without restraint. That can sound grim, so look closely. He isn't banning joy. The worry seems to be the kind of laughing that runs away with a person: laughing to fit in, laughing at someone, laughing so loudly that you're no longer really there. A smile you mean is still in your power. A roar to impress the room may not be. Second, oaths. Refuse to swear an oath, he says, altogether if you can, and if you can't, as far as you can. He doesn't stop to explain. Third, one way to read it. If your plain word is good, an oath adds nothing. If your plain word isn't good, an oath won't fix it. Piling on swears is a quiet admission that a simple yes isn't enough. So the Stoic aims to be the kind of person whose yes is the whole promise. Fourth, a neighbor who said something close. In the Sermon on the Mount, in the King James Bible, Jesus says: "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay." Christians have taken that in different ways. Quakers, and some Mennonite and Amish communities, decline to swear oaths and affirm instead. Other Christians take oaths in court and office and read the verse as being about honesty. The United States Constitution makes room for both: a president may swear, or affirm. Two traditions, each in its own house, arriving at the same plain picture: a word that doesn't need help.
screen: `DON'T LAUGH MUCH, OR WITHOUT RESTRAINT.` · `REFUSE OATHS, AS FAR AS YOU CAN.` · `A GOOD WORD NEEDS NO OATH.` · `YEA, YEA; NAY, NAY.` · then, large: `YES MEANS YES.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one promise you've made recently, small or large. I'll call you back. I'll finish it by Friday. I'll be there. Picture the person you made it to. Now, without adding a single I swear, just decide to keep it. Feel how plain that is: no drama, no extra words, just a yes that holds. If there's a promise you can't keep, picture yourself telling them so, simply. The bell holds the time.
Oath. What Epictetus says to refuse as far as you can, letting your plain word carry the promise instead. Today's word.
Your line: a word that doesn't need help. Keep one promise today without swearing, stacking, or hand-on-heart. Just say yes, and do it. Day three hundred sixty-six.

pairs: refuse them as far as you can

options: swear by everything you hold dear.

fork.reveal: he says refuse oaths as far as you can. a good word needs no oath, and a bad one isn't fixed by it.

what it means: laugh without losing yourself, and let your plain word be your promise.

367.title: Ask, don't tell
367.hook: don't dwell on your own deeds and dangers; others don't enjoy them as you do (Enchiridion 33)
367.carry: hands the stage to someone else
367.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes set themselves a simple conversational habit: fewer stories about their own exploits and more questions about the other person.

segments.voice: Yesterday: oaths, laughter, and the plain word. Your line was a word that doesn't need help. Which promise did you keep without swearing? Day three hundred sixty-seven.

Everyone has been on the receiving end of this. Dinner, a long table, and someone is telling the story of their near miss on the highway. Or the marathon. Or the time they told the boss exactly what they thought. It's the third time you've heard it, and it's getting longer. And here's the uncomfortable part: everyone has also been the one telling it. Section thirty-three, still sketching how to behave in company, has a line for exactly this. Today: ask, don't tell.
screen: `DINNER, AND THE NEAR-MISS STORY.` → `THE THIRD TIME YOU'VE HEARD IT.` → `ASK, DON'T TELL.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. In company, Epictetus says, don't keep bringing up your own deeds and your own dangers, often and at length. Second, the reason, and it's disarmingly honest. However pleasant it is for you to recall your dangers, it isn't as pleasant for other people to hear about them. That's it. No grand theory. Just an observation anyone can check at the next dinner party. Our own stories glow for us because we were in them. For everyone else, they're secondhand. Third, the line that comes right after. Avoid playing for laughs, he says. It slides easily into vulgarity, and it tends to lower the respect the people around you have for you. The common thread is the spotlight. Telling your adventures and working the room for a laugh both turn a conversation into a stage with one performer. Fourth, the turn. The handbook doesn't say ask in so many words; that's how this path carries it. But it fits the man Epictetus admired most. Socrates, in Plato's dialogues, is famous for asking questions, so many that it became a method named after him. If you're not telling, you have room to ask. How was your week? What happened next? What was that like for you? A question hands the stage to someone else. It's a small trade: one story fewer told, one more heard all the way to the end.
screen: `DON'T DWELL ON YOUR OWN EXPLOITS.` · `YOUR DANGERS THRILL YOU, NOT THEM.` · `DON'T PLAY FOR LAUGHS.` · `SOCRATES ASKED.` · then, large: `ASK, DON'T TELL.`

segments.voice: Sit back, and breathe. Think of someone you'll talk with today: a coworker, a friend, a parent, a child, the person at the counter. Picture the moment you'd usually start telling them your news. Now picture asking them a question instead, and actually waiting for the answer. Which question? How are you, really. What's been the best part of your week. What are you working on. Choose one and keep it ready. The bell holds the time.
Ask. Enchiridion thirty-three: don't keep telling your own deeds and dangers. Others don't enjoy them as much as you do. Leave room to ask. Today's word.
Your line: hands the stage to someone else. In one conversation today, ask more and tell less. Ask a real question, and let the answer have the floor. Day three hundred sixty-seven.

368.title: He missed the rest
368.hook: if told someone speaks ill of you, say: he didn't know my other faults (Enchiridion 33)
368.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes answer reported criticism with self-deprecating humor, as Epictetus suggests, rather than defending themselves point by point.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your own deeds and dangers, which please you more than your listeners. Your line was hands the stage to someone else. What question did you ask, and what did you hear? Day three hundred sixty-eight.
screen: `ASK — HANDS THE STAGE TO SOMEONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: A screenshot arrives with a short note above it: thought you should know. Someone has been saying things about you. It's easy to start drafting the reply right there in your head, point by point, with receipts and a closing line. Section thirty-three of the handbook has a one-line answer for this moment, far older than any screenshot. It's short, it's a little ridiculous, and it's a very good comeback. Today: he missed the rest.
screen: `THOUGHT YOU SHOULD KNOW.` → `ALREADY DRAFTING THE REPLY.` → `HE MISSED THE REST.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. If someone tells you that a certain person is speaking badly of you, Epictetus says, don't defend yourself against what was said. Instead, answer: he obviously didn't know my other faults, or he wouldn't have mentioned only these. Second, why it works. A defense keeps the argument alive. You go point by point, they answer, the circle grows. Epictetus' reply steps out of the contest entirely. It agrees, cheerfully, that you have faults, more than the critic knows, and so there's nothing left to fight about. The joke is on yourself, and nobody else gets hurt by it. Third, the Greek. The verb he uses for defend yourself belongs with apologia, a speech of defense, the word in the title of Plato's Apology, where Socrates defends himself at his trial. Epictetus' advice, roughly: skip the apologia. Fourth, what it isn't. It isn't self-hatred, and it isn't ignoring a fair point. If the critic is right about something, you've learned something. If they're wrong, nothing that belongs to you has been touched. We met that idea a couple of weeks ago, with the insult: it's not the words that harm you, but your judgment that you've been harmed. Today's line is that idea with a grin on its face. It costs nothing. And it ends the conversation better than any receipt.
screen: `DON'T DEFEND YOURSELF.` · `HE DIDN'T KNOW MY OTHER FAULTS.` · `SKIP THE APOLOGIA.` · `A FAIR POINT TEACHES; A WRONG ONE CAN'T HARM.` · then, large: `HE MISSED THE REST.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and breathe. Bring to mind one criticism that still stings, something said about you or to you, recently or long ago. Notice where it lands in your body. Notice the urge to argue with it. Now try Epictetus' answer, quietly, inside: he missed the rest. You might even smile. See if the sting changes. If part of the criticism was fair, let that part stay, and let the rest go. The bell holds the time.
Apologia. The Greek word for a speech of defense, which Epictetus says to skip: they didn't know my other faults, or they'd have mentioned those too. Today's word.
Your line: better than any receipt. If a criticism reaches you today, answer it with humor instead of a defense, out loud or just inside. Day three hundred sixty-eight.

369.title: Wait before pleasure
369.hook: when a pleasure beckons, pause, and picture both the enjoying and the regret after (Enchiridion 34)
369.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism put a short delay between an urge and acting on it, and in that pause picture both the enjoyment and how they'll feel afterward.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the critic, and the joke that ends the contest. Your line was better than any receipt. Did a criticism come your way, and did you laugh? Day three hundred sixty-nine.

The kitchen is dark except for the open fridge, and the last slice of cake is right there. Or it's the tab with the shopping cart, or the one more episode button counting down from ten. There's a moment, maybe half a second long, between the urge showing up and your hand moving. It's easy to miss that half second entirely. Section thirty-four of the handbook lives entirely inside it, and asks you to stretch it out. Today: wait before pleasure.
screen: `THE OPEN FRIDGE, THE LAST SLICE.` → `HALF A SECOND BEFORE THE HAND MOVES.` → `WAIT BEFORE PLEASURE.`

segments.voice: First, the guard. When the impression of some pleasure arrives, Epictetus says, be careful not to be swept off by it. Let the thing wait for you. Give yourself a little delay. Notice he doesn't say refuse. He says wait. Second, two pictures. In the delay, he says, call to mind two times. The time when you'll be enjoying the pleasure. And the time after, when you've had it, and you're sorry, and you're scolding yourself. Both are real. Look at both. Third, a third picture to set against them: how glad you'll be, and how you'll think well of yourself, if you hold off. Three scenes, and you get to watch all of them before you choose. Fourth, the honest ending. If, after all that, it seems the right time to enjoy the thing, Epictetus allows it. Just take care, he says, that its sweetness and its pull don't overpower you, and remember how much better it is to know you've won that small contest. This isn't a rule against pleasure. It's a rule against being carried. The pleasure that survives the wait is one you've chosen. Stretch the half second into a few minutes, and the one deciding has had time to look at all three pictures.
screen: `LET THE PLEASURE WAIT FOR YOU.` · `PICTURE THE ENJOYING, AND THE REGRET.` · `PICTURE THE GLADNESS OF HOLDING OFF.` · `IF YOU TAKE IT, DON'T BE CARRIED.` · then, large: `WAIT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of an urge you know well: a snack, a scroll, a purchase, a drink, a reply typed too fast. Picture it arriving. Now run Epictetus' three pictures, slowly. The enjoying. The after, and how you might feel. And the gladness of having waited. You don't need to decide anything now. Just practice watching all three before your hand moves. The bell holds the time.
Wait before pleasure. Epictetus' advice to let a pleasure wait, picture the enjoying and the regret, and choose instead of being carried. Today's word.
Your line: wait. When one urge shows up today, wait ten minutes before you act on it. Then choose. Day three hundred sixty-nine.

370.title: No need to hide
370.hook: if you've judged it right, don't hide doing it (Enchiridion 35)
370.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes check whether they are hiding a right action out of fear of disapproval, and if so, do it openly; if the wish to hide signals that the act is wrong, they don't do it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the urge, the delay, and three pictures before the hand moves. Your line was wait. Which urge did you wait out, and what did you choose? Day three hundred seventy.

A teenager in a school cafeteria sees the new kid eating alone. She'd like to go sit with him. She'd also like nobody to see her do it. A man leaves the office at five sharp to coach his daughter's soccer team, and he slips out the side door so the others won't notice. We do the right thing, and then we do it a little bit in hiding, as if we've been caught. Section thirty-five of the handbook is only a few lines long, and it's aimed at exactly that side door. Today: no need to hide.
screen: `THE NEW KID EATING ALONE.` → `OUT THE SIDE DOOR AT FIVE.` → `NO NEED TO HIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the line. When you've judged that something ought to be done, and you're doing it, Epictetus says, never avoid being seen doing it, even if the many are going to think badly of it. Second, the logic, and it's tidy. Either the thing is wrong, or it's right. If it's wrong, don't do it at all. If it's right, then the people who'll find fault with it are mistaken, so why be afraid of them? Hiding a right action quietly hands a vote to people whose opinion, by your own judgment, is wrong. Third, an echo from earlier in the handbook. Weeks ago, section thirteen asked us to be content to seem foolish about outside things, and section twenty-two warned that anyone who takes up this way of life will be laughed at. Today's line is the practical follow-through. You've already accepted that people may think you odd. So stop ducking. Fourth, a useful test hidden inside the sentence. If you notice the urge to hide something you're doing, ask why. Sometimes it's only fear of what people will say, and Epictetus' answer is: then do it in the open. But sometimes the wish to hide is the first quiet sign that the thing isn't right, and his answer to that is just as plain: then don't do it. This isn't about showing off. The handbook will get to that soon. It's about not shrinking. A right thing done openly also gives the next person permission to do it too.
screen: `JUDGED RIGHT? DON'T AVOID BEING SEEN.` · `WRONG: DON'T. RIGHT: WHY FEAR CRITICS?` · `YOU'VE ALREADY ACCEPTED SEEMING ODD.` · `THE URGE TO HIDE IS A TEST.` · then, large: `NO NEED TO HIDE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and breathe. Think of one right thing you do a little sheepishly. Leaving on time for your family. Saying no to a drink. Bowing your head before a meal. Asking a question in a meeting. Sitting with someone others avoid. Picture yourself doing it today, in plain view, at an ordinary pace. No apology, no announcement. Notice whether the urge to hide shows up, and what it's made of. The bell holds the time.
The many. Epictetus' name for the people whose disapproval needn't be feared; if you've judged it right, don't avoid being seen doing it. Today's word.
Your line: without the side door. Do one right thing openly today, at an ordinary pace. Day three hundred seventy.

371.title: The table matters
371.hook: the biggest portion may suit your stomach, but not the fellowship of the table (Enchiridion 36)
371.carry: for the sake of the fellowship
371.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism take the smaller share at shared meals and let others choose first, as a small way of honoring the company and the host.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the side door, and the right thing done in plain view. Your line was without the side door. What did you do openly? Day three hundred seventy-one.

A platter comes around the table. Four pieces of chicken left, and one of them is clearly the biggest. Everyone sees it. Everyone pretends not to. There's a small, silent negotiation going on, and you may have been on both sides of it. Epictetus, of all people, uses this moment to teach a bit of logic. Section thirty-six starts like a textbook on reasoning and ends at a dinner party. Today, to close the week: the table matters.
screen: `FOUR PIECES LEFT. ONE IS BIGGEST.` → `A LOGIC LESSON AT DINNER.` → `THE TABLE MATTERS.`

segments.voice: First, the logic. Take two statements: it is day, it is night. Joined with or, it is day or it is night, they make a perfectly good statement. Joined with and, it is day and it is night, they make a false one. Same pieces. Different combination. The value depends on how they're joined. Second, the dinner. In the same way, Epictetus says, at a shared meal, taking the biggest portion may have value for your body taken alone. But joined to the table, to the company and the host, it loses that value. So the larger share is to be avoided, for the sake of the fellowship of the meal. Third, what to look at. When you eat with someone, he says, don't only weigh what the food on your plate is worth to your body. Keep in view the respect owed to your host. The meal is not just food. It's a relationship being kept, one plate at a time. Fourth, why a Stoic cares. Back in section fifteen, life was a banquet, and we learned to take a modest share when the dish reaches us. Today goes one step further. The smaller portion isn't only self-control. It's a way of honoring the people at the table. And a look back at the week, since today closes it: mostly quiet. Yes means yes. Ask, don't tell. He missed the rest. Wait. No need to hide. Every one of them, like today's, is about living well alongside other people.
screen: `DAY OR NIGHT: TRUE. DAY AND NIGHT: FALSE.` · `THE BIGGEST PORTION, JOINED TO THE TABLE.` · `KEEP THE HOST IN VIEW.` · `THE SMALLER PORTION HONORS THE TABLE.` · then, large: `THE TABLE MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Picture the next meal you'll share with someone, at home, at work, anywhere. See the table, the faces, the food going around. Now see yourself, quietly, taking the smaller portion, or letting someone else choose first. No announcement. Notice how it feels to put the table ahead of your plate for a moment. Then let the picture go, and just breathe. The bell holds the time.
Banquet. Life as a shared meal, Epictetus says elsewhere; the biggest portion may suit your body, but not the fellowship of the table. Today's word.
Your line: for the sake of the fellowship. At one shared meal today, take the smaller portion, or let someone else choose first. Day three hundred seventy-one.

fork.setup: the platter reaches you. four pieces left, one clearly biggest. what does Epictetus suggest?
options: take the biggest. it's good for your body.
leave the biggest, for the sake of the table and the host.
take two, so nobody has to choose.
fork.reveal: the big portion may suit the body, he says, but keep the fellowship of the meal and the respect owed the host in view.

original.note: Greek: a drinking party or banquet, where English symposium comes from; Epictetus' shared meal.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be greedy.
what it means: a thing good for you alone can be bad joined to others; the shared table changes its value.
what a scholar hears: Stoic logic, an or-statement versus an and-statement, applied to who takes the biggest portion at dinner.
